These exercises go with [Module 4: Spectral and time-frequency analysis](../modules/04-spectral-analysis.qmd). They cover the practical side of frequency-domain analysis: computing power spectral density, extracting power in the standard EEG bands, tracking how spectral content changes over time, and comparing spectral features between groups. All exercises use simulated data so you always know the ground truth.

## Exercise 1: Compute PSD with Welch's method and identify peaks

Create a simulated signal that combines a 10 Hz alpha oscillation, a 22 Hz beta oscillation, and pink (1/f) background noise. Compute the power spectral density using `scipy.signal.welch` and plot it. Identify the two spectral peaks and label them on the plot.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Generate pink noise by filtering white noise in the frequency domain: take the FFT, scale each frequency bin by $1/\sqrt{f}$ (to get a $1/f$ power spectrum), then take the inverse FFT. Add two sine waves at 10 Hz and 22 Hz with different amplitudes (alpha is usually stronger than beta). For Welch's method, use `scipy.signal.welch(signal, fs=sfreq, nperseg=512)`. Plot on a log scale (`ax.semilogy()`) so both peaks are visible above the 1/f background.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{python}
#| eval: false
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import signal

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

sfreq = 256
duration = 30
n_samples = sfreq * duration
times = np.arange(n_samples) / sfreq

# Generate pink noise (1/f background)
white = rng.standard_normal(n_samples)
freqs_fft = np.fft.rfftfreq(n_samples, d=1 / sfreq)
freqs_fft[0] = 1  # avoid division by zero
pink_filter = 1 / np.sqrt(freqs_fft)
pink = np.fft.irfft(np.fft.rfft(white) * pink_filter, n=n_samples)
pink = pink / pink.std()

# Add oscillatory components
alpha = 1.5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times)   # 10 Hz alpha
beta = 0.7 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 22 * times)    # 22 Hz beta (weaker)
eeg = pink + alpha + beta

# Compute PSD with Welch's method
freqs_psd, psd = signal.welch(eeg, fs=sfreq, nperseg=512, noverlap=256)

# Plot
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.semilogy(freqs_psd, psd, linewidth=1.2, color="#2c3e50")
ax.axvline(10, color="#e74c3c", linestyle="--", alpha=0.7, label="Alpha (10 Hz)")
ax.axvline(22, color="#3498db", linestyle="--", alpha=0.7, label="Beta (22 Hz)")
ax.set_xlabel("Frequency (Hz)")
ax.set_ylabel("Power spectral density")
ax.set_title("PSD of simulated EEG (alpha + beta + pink noise)")
ax.set_xlim(0, 50)
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

You should see the characteristic 1/f slope of the pink noise with two peaks rising above it: a taller one at 10 Hz and a shorter one at 22 Hz. The log scale on the y-axis makes both peaks easy to spot, even though the alpha component has roughly twice the amplitude of the beta component.
:::


## Exercise 2: Compute band power and relative power for the five standard bands

Create a simulated signal with a strong alpha peak (similar to Exercise 1) and compute the absolute power in each of the five standard EEG frequency bands: delta (0.5--4 Hz), theta (4--8 Hz), alpha (8--13 Hz), beta (13--30 Hz), and gamma (30--45 Hz). Then compute the relative power of each band as a percentage of the total power across all bands. Print a table of results.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
After computing the PSD with `scipy.signal.welch`, use `np.trapezoid()` (or `scipy.integrate.trapezoid()`) to integrate the PSD over each frequency range. To select the right frequencies, create a boolean mask: `mask = (freqs >= f_low) & (freqs < f_high)`. Relative power is simply `band_power / total_power * 100`. Total power is the sum of all five bands (or the integral over the full range).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{python}
#| eval: false
import numpy as np
from scipy import signal

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

sfreq = 256
duration = 60
n_samples = sfreq * duration
times = np.arange(n_samples) / sfreq

# Signal: pink noise + alpha oscillation + some beta
white = rng.standard_normal(n_samples)
freqs_fft = np.fft.rfftfreq(n_samples, d=1 / sfreq)
freqs_fft[0] = 1
pink_filter = 1 / np.sqrt(freqs_fft)
pink = np.fft.irfft(np.fft.rfft(white) * pink_filter, n=n_samples)
pink = pink / pink.std()

alpha = 2.0 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times)
beta = 0.5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 20 * times)
eeg = pink + alpha + beta

# Compute PSD
freqs_psd, psd = signal.welch(eeg, fs=sfreq, nperseg=1024, noverlap=512)

# Define the standard EEG bands
bands = {
    "Delta": (0.5, 4),
    "Theta": (4, 8),
    "Alpha": (8, 13),
    "Beta":  (13, 30),
    "Gamma": (30, 45),
}

# Compute absolute band power by integrating the PSD
band_powers = {}
for name, (f_low, f_high) in bands.items():
    mask = (freqs_psd >= f_low) & (freqs_psd < f_high)
    band_powers[name] = np.trapezoid(psd[mask], freqs_psd[mask])

total_power = sum(band_powers.values())

# Print the results
print(f"{'Band':<8} {'Abs. power':>12} {'Rel. power (%)':>15}")
print("-" * 38)
for name, power in band_powers.items():
    rel = power / total_power * 100
    print(f"{name:<8} {power:>12.4f} {rel:>14.1f}%")
print("-" * 38)
print(f"{'Total':<8} {total_power:>12.4f} {'100.0%':>15}")
```

Alpha should dominate because we injected a strong 10 Hz oscillation. Delta will also have a fair share because the 1/f pink noise concentrates power at low frequencies. Beta and gamma should be low, and theta will be somewhere in between.
:::


## Exercise 3: Visualise time-varying alpha power with a spectrogram

Create a 20-second signal where alpha power is strong in the first 10 seconds and weak (or absent) in the last 10 seconds, simulating an "eyes closed then eyes open" transition. Use `scipy.signal.spectrogram` to compute and plot the spectrogram. Verify that the alpha band (8--13 Hz) shows a clear drop at the midpoint.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Build the signal in two halves: for the first half, add a large-amplitude 10 Hz sine wave to the noise; for the second half, use noise only (or add a much smaller sine wave). `scipy.signal.spectrogram` returns `(frequencies, times, Sxx)` where `Sxx[i, j]` is the power at `frequencies[i]` and `times[j]`. Plot it with `ax.pcolormesh(times, frequencies, 10 * np.log10(Sxx))` for a dB scale. Use `nperseg=256` and `noverlap=128` for reasonable time-frequency resolution at 256 Hz sampling rate.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{python}
#| eval: false
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import signal

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

sfreq = 256
duration = 20
n_samples = sfreq * duration
times = np.arange(n_samples) / sfreq
midpoint = n_samples // 2

# Background noise for the full signal
noise = rng.standard_normal(n_samples) * 0.5

# Alpha oscillation: strong in first half, absent in second half
alpha = np.zeros(n_samples)
alpha[:midpoint] = 2.0 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times[:midpoint])

eeg = noise + alpha

# Compute the spectrogram
freqs_spec, times_spec, Sxx = signal.spectrogram(
    eeg, fs=sfreq, nperseg=256, noverlap=128
)

# Plot
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10, 7))

# Top panel: time-domain signal
ax = axes[0]
ax.plot(times, eeg, linewidth=0.3, color="#2c3e50")
ax.axvline(10, color="#e74c3c", linestyle="--", alpha=0.7, label="Transition")
ax.set_xlabel("Time (s)")
ax.set_ylabel("Amplitude (a.u.)")
ax.set_title("Simulated EEG: strong alpha (0-10 s), then noise only (10-20 s)")
ax.legend()

# Bottom panel: spectrogram
ax = axes[1]
mesh = ax.pcolormesh(
    times_spec, freqs_spec, 10 * np.log10(Sxx),
    shading="gouraud", cmap="viridis"
)
ax.set_ylim(0, 40)
ax.axhline(8, color="white", linestyle="--", linewidth=0.7, alpha=0.7)
ax.axhline(13, color="white", linestyle="--", linewidth=0.7, alpha=0.7)
ax.set_xlabel("Time (s)")
ax.set_ylabel("Frequency (Hz)")
ax.set_title("Spectrogram (dB)")
fig.colorbar(mesh, ax=ax, label="Power (dB)")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The spectrogram should show a bright horizontal band between 8 and 13 Hz in the first half of the recording, which disappears abruptly at the 10-second mark. The white dashed lines mark the alpha band boundaries. This is the spectral signature of alpha desynchronisation, which is what happens in real EEG when someone opens their eyes.
:::


## Exercise 4: Compare PSD between two simulated groups

Simulate two "groups" of subjects. Group A has a strong alpha peak (10 Hz); Group B has a weak alpha peak. Generate 15 subjects per group, compute the alpha band power for each, and run an independent-samples t-test to determine whether the groups differ significantly. Plot the group-averaged PSDs and a box plot of alpha band power.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
For each subject, generate a fresh noise signal and add a 10 Hz sine wave with a group-specific amplitude (e.g., amplitude = 2.0 for Group A, amplitude = 0.5 for Group B, plus some between-subject variability drawn from a normal distribution). Compute the PSD for each subject with `scipy.signal.welch`, then integrate across the alpha band (8--13 Hz) to get one band-power value per subject. Use `scipy.stats.ttest_ind` for the t-test.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{python}
#| eval: false
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import signal
from scipy.stats import ttest_ind

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

sfreq = 256
duration = 60
n_samples = sfreq * duration
times = np.arange(n_samples) / sfreq
n_subjects = 15

def simulate_subject(alpha_amp, rng):
    """Simulate one subject's EEG and return alpha band power."""
    # Pink noise
    white = rng.standard_normal(n_samples)
    freqs_fft = np.fft.rfftfreq(n_samples, d=1 / sfreq)
    freqs_fft[0] = 1
    pink_filter = 1 / np.sqrt(freqs_fft)
    pink = np.fft.irfft(np.fft.rfft(white) * pink_filter, n=n_samples)
    pink = pink / pink.std()

    # Add alpha oscillation
    eeg = pink + alpha_amp * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times)

    # Compute PSD
    freqs_psd, psd = signal.welch(eeg, fs=sfreq, nperseg=1024, noverlap=512)
    return freqs_psd, psd

# Simulate both groups
alpha_powers_a = []
alpha_powers_b = []
psds_a = []
psds_b = []

for i in range(n_subjects):
    # Group A: strong alpha (mean amplitude 2.0, sd 0.3)
    amp_a = rng.normal(2.0, 0.3)
    freqs_psd, psd_a = simulate_subject(amp_a, rng)
    psds_a.append(psd_a)
    mask_alpha = (freqs_psd >= 8) & (freqs_psd < 13)
    alpha_powers_a.append(np.trapezoid(psd_a[mask_alpha], freqs_psd[mask_alpha]))

    # Group B: weak alpha (mean amplitude 0.5, sd 0.2)
    amp_b = rng.normal(0.5, 0.2)
    freqs_psd, psd_b = simulate_subject(amp_b, rng)
    psds_b.append(psd_b)
    alpha_powers_b.append(np.trapezoid(psd_b[mask_alpha], freqs_psd[mask_alpha]))

alpha_powers_a = np.array(alpha_powers_a)
alpha_powers_b = np.array(alpha_powers_b)

# T-test
t_stat, p_value = ttest_ind(alpha_powers_a, alpha_powers_b)
print(f"Group A alpha power: mean = {alpha_powers_a.mean():.3f}, "
      f"sd = {alpha_powers_a.std():.3f}")
print(f"Group B alpha power: mean = {alpha_powers_b.mean():.3f}, "
      f"sd = {alpha_powers_b.std():.3f}")
print(f"t-test: t = {t_stat:.3f}, p = {p_value:.6f}")

# Plot
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5))

# Left: group-averaged PSDs
ax = axes[0]
mean_psd_a = np.mean(psds_a, axis=0)
mean_psd_b = np.mean(psds_b, axis=0)
ax.semilogy(freqs_psd, mean_psd_a, label="Group A (strong alpha)",
            color="#e74c3c", linewidth=1.5)
ax.semilogy(freqs_psd, mean_psd_b, label="Group B (weak alpha)",
            color="#3498db", linewidth=1.5)
ax.axvspan(8, 13, alpha=0.15, color="orange", label="Alpha band")
ax.set_xlabel("Frequency (Hz)")
ax.set_ylabel("PSD")
ax.set_xlim(0, 45)
ax.set_title("Group-averaged PSD")
ax.legend(fontsize=9)

# Right: box plot of alpha band power
ax = axes[1]
bp = ax.boxplot(
    [alpha_powers_a, alpha_powers_b],
    labels=["Group A\n(strong alpha)", "Group B\n(weak alpha)"],
    patch_artist=True
)
bp["boxes"][0].set_facecolor("#e74c3c")
bp["boxes"][1].set_facecolor("#3498db")
for box in bp["boxes"]:
    box.set_alpha(0.5)
ax.set_ylabel("Alpha band power (8-13 Hz)")
ax.set_title(f"Alpha power comparison (p = {p_value:.2e})")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

You should see a highly significant p-value (well below 0.05) because the two groups have very different alpha amplitudes by design. The PSD plot will show Group A with a tall alpha peak and Group B with a much smaller one. In real studies, the effect sizes are usually much smaller, but the analysis workflow is the same.
:::


## Exercise 5: Build a reusable band-power function

Write a function `compute_band_powers(data, sfreq)` that takes a 2D NumPy array (channels x samples) and a sampling rate, and returns a dictionary where each key is a band name (`"delta"`, `"theta"`, `"alpha"`, `"beta"`, `"gamma"`) and each value is a 1D array of band powers (one value per channel). Test it on a simulated multi-channel signal and print the results.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Inside the function, loop over channels and compute the PSD for each one using `scipy.signal.welch`. Then, for each band, integrate the PSD between the band's frequency limits using `np.trapezoid`. Return a dictionary of arrays. You could also compute the PSD for all channels at once by passing a 2D array to `scipy.signal.welch` (it operates along the last axis by default, so you may need to handle the axis parameter).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{python}
#| eval: false
import numpy as np
from scipy import signal


BANDS = {
    "delta": (0.5, 4),
    "theta": (4, 8),
    "alpha": (8, 13),
    "beta":  (13, 30),
    "gamma": (30, 45),
}


def compute_band_powers(data, sfreq, nperseg=1024):
    """Compute band power for each channel in the standard EEG bands.

    Parameters
    ----------
    data : numpy.ndarray
        2D array of shape (n_channels, n_samples).
    sfreq : float
        Sampling frequency in Hz.
    nperseg : int
        Number of samples per Welch segment (controls frequency resolution).

    Returns
    -------
    band_powers : dict
        Keys are band names ('delta', 'theta', 'alpha', 'beta', 'gamma').
        Values are 1D arrays of shape (n_channels,) with the band power
        for each channel.
    """
    n_channels = data.shape[0]
    band_powers = {name: np.zeros(n_channels) for name in BANDS}

    for ch in range(n_channels):
        freqs_psd, psd = signal.welch(
            data[ch], fs=sfreq, nperseg=nperseg, noverlap=nperseg // 2
        )
        for name, (f_low, f_high) in BANDS.items():
            mask = (freqs_psd >= f_low) & (freqs_psd < f_high)
            band_powers[name][ch] = np.trapezoid(psd[mask], freqs_psd[mask])

    return band_powers


# ── Test the function ──────────────────────────────────────────
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

sfreq = 256
duration = 30
n_samples = sfreq * duration
times = np.arange(n_samples) / sfreq

ch_names = ["Fp1", "Fp2", "C3", "C4", "O1", "O2", "Oz", "Pz"]
n_channels = len(ch_names)

# Simulate data: noise + alpha in occipital channels + beta in central
data = rng.standard_normal((n_channels, n_samples)) * 0.5

# Add alpha to O1, O2, Oz
for ch_name in ["O1", "O2", "Oz"]:
    idx = ch_names.index(ch_name)
    data[idx] += 2.0 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times)

# Add beta to C3, C4
for ch_name in ["C3", "C4"]:
    idx = ch_names.index(ch_name)
    data[idx] += 1.0 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 20 * times)

# Compute band powers
bp = compute_band_powers(data, sfreq)

# Print the results
print(f"{'Channel':<8}", end="")
for name in BANDS:
    print(f"{name:>10}", end="")
print()
print("-" * 58)
for ch in range(n_channels):
    print(f"{ch_names[ch]:<8}", end="")
    for name in BANDS:
        print(f"{bp[name][ch]:>10.4f}", end="")
    print()
```

The occipital channels (O1, O2, Oz) should show high alpha power relative to the others. The central channels (C3, C4) should show higher beta power. Frontal channels (Fp1, Fp2) and Pz will only have noise, so their band powers should be roughly uniform and much lower.
:::


## Exercise 6: Effect of window length on PSD resolution

Create a signal that combines two close sine waves at 9 Hz and 11 Hz (plus some noise). Compute the PSD with Welch's method four times, using `nperseg` values of 256, 512, 1024, and 2048. Plot all four PSDs on the same figure. You should see that short windows blur the two peaks into one, while longer windows can separate them. This demonstrates the trade-off between frequency resolution and the number of averaged segments.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Frequency resolution is approximately `sfreq / nperseg`. With `sfreq = 256` and `nperseg = 256`, the resolution is 1 Hz, which is not enough to separate peaks that are only 2 Hz apart (you need better than 2 Hz resolution, but the spectral leakage from a 1 Hz bin width will merge them). With `nperseg = 2048`, resolution is 0.125 Hz, which easily resolves two peaks 2 Hz apart. Use subplots or overlay the four PSDs with a legend.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{python}
#| eval: false
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import signal

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

sfreq = 256
duration = 30
n_samples = sfreq * duration
times = np.arange(n_samples) / sfreq

# Two close peaks at 9 Hz and 11 Hz, plus noise
sig = (1.5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 9 * times)
       + 1.5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 11 * times)
       + rng.standard_normal(n_samples) * 0.8)

# Compute PSD with different window lengths
nperseg_values = [256, 512, 1024, 2048]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 8), sharex=True, sharey=True)
axes = axes.ravel()

for ax, nperseg in zip(axes, nperseg_values):
    freqs_psd, psd = signal.welch(sig, fs=sfreq, nperseg=nperseg,
                                  noverlap=nperseg // 2)
    freq_res = sfreq / nperseg
    ax.plot(freqs_psd, psd, linewidth=1.2, color="#2c3e50")
    ax.axvline(9, color="#e74c3c", linestyle="--", alpha=0.6, linewidth=0.8)
    ax.axvline(11, color="#3498db", linestyle="--", alpha=0.6, linewidth=0.8)
    ax.set_xlim(4, 18)
    ax.set_title(f"nperseg = {nperseg}  (resolution = {freq_res:.2f} Hz)")
    ax.set_xlabel("Frequency (Hz)")
    ax.set_ylabel("PSD")

fig.suptitle("Effect of window length on frequency resolution", fontsize=13)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Print frequency resolution for each setting
for nperseg in nperseg_values:
    print(f"nperseg = {nperseg:>5d}  ->  freq. resolution = "
          f"{sfreq / nperseg:.3f} Hz")
```

With `nperseg = 256` (1 Hz resolution), the two peaks merge into a single broad hump centred around 10 Hz. At `nperseg = 512` (0.5 Hz), you may start to see a hint of two peaks. At `nperseg = 1024` and `nperseg = 2048`, the two peaks at 9 Hz and 11 Hz are clearly separated. The cost of using longer windows is that you get fewer segments to average, so the PSD estimate is noisier.
:::


## Exercise 7: Find the individual alpha frequency (IAF)

Create a simulated EEG signal where the alpha peak sits at 10.5 Hz rather than exactly 10 Hz (this is realistic, since the individual alpha frequency varies from person to person, typically between 8 and 13 Hz). Compute the PSD with Welch's method and then find the exact peak frequency in the 8--13 Hz range by locating the frequency bin with the maximum power. Print the detected IAF and compare it with the true value.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Generate pink noise and add a sine wave at 10.5 Hz. After computing the PSD, create a boolean mask for the alpha range (`(freqs >= 8) & (freqs <= 13)`), then use `np.argmax(psd[mask])` to find the index of the peak within that range. The corresponding frequency is `freqs[mask][peak_index]`. Use a long `nperseg` (e.g., 2048) to get enough frequency resolution to distinguish 10.5 Hz from 10.0 Hz.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{python}
#| eval: false
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import signal

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

sfreq = 256
duration = 60
n_samples = sfreq * duration
times = np.arange(n_samples) / sfreq
true_iaf = 10.5  # Hz

# Pink noise background
white = rng.standard_normal(n_samples)
freqs_fft = np.fft.rfftfreq(n_samples, d=1 / sfreq)
freqs_fft[0] = 1  # avoid division by zero
pink_filter = 1 / np.sqrt(freqs_fft)
pink = np.fft.irfft(np.fft.rfft(white) * pink_filter, n=n_samples)
pink = pink / pink.std()

# Add alpha oscillation at 10.5 Hz
alpha = 2.0 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * true_iaf * times)
eeg = pink + alpha

# Compute PSD with good frequency resolution
freqs_psd, psd = signal.welch(eeg, fs=sfreq, nperseg=2048, noverlap=1024)

# Find peak in the alpha range
alpha_mask = (freqs_psd >= 8) & (freqs_psd <= 13)
alpha_freqs = freqs_psd[alpha_mask]
alpha_psd = psd[alpha_mask]
peak_idx = np.argmax(alpha_psd)
detected_iaf = alpha_freqs[peak_idx]

print(f"True IAF:     {true_iaf:.2f} Hz")
print(f"Detected IAF: {detected_iaf:.2f} Hz")
print(f"Error:        {abs(detected_iaf - true_iaf):.3f} Hz")

# Plot
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.semilogy(freqs_psd, psd, linewidth=1.2, color="#2c3e50")
ax.axvline(detected_iaf, color="#e74c3c", linestyle="--",
           label=f"Detected IAF = {detected_iaf:.2f} Hz")
ax.axvspan(8, 13, alpha=0.15, color="orange", label="Alpha band")
ax.set_xlim(0, 40)
ax.set_xlabel("Frequency (Hz)")
ax.set_ylabel("PSD")
ax.set_title("Individual alpha frequency detection")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The detected IAF should be very close to 10.5 Hz (the error depends on the frequency resolution, which is `256 / 2048 = 0.125 Hz` here). In real EEG data, researchers use the IAF to define subject-specific alpha bands (e.g., IAF +/- 2 Hz) rather than using the fixed 8--13 Hz range for everyone.
:::


## Exercise 8: Estimate the 1/f aperiodic slope

Create pink noise with a known 1/f exponent. In the frequency domain, pink noise has a power spectrum that falls off as $1/f^\beta$, where $\beta = 1$ for classical pink noise. Compute the PSD, take the logarithm of both the frequencies and the PSD values, and fit a straight line using `np.polyfit`. The slope of that line is your estimate of $-\beta$. Compare it with the known ground truth. This is the basis of spectral parameterisation methods like FOOOF/specparam.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
To generate noise with a specific exponent $\beta$, take white noise, compute its FFT, multiply each frequency bin by $f^{-\beta/2}$ (since power is amplitude squared), then take the inverse FFT. For the fit, work in log-log space: `log_f = np.log10(freqs)` and `log_psd = np.log10(psd)`. Exclude the DC component (frequency 0) and very high frequencies (above 45 Hz or so) where noise dominates. Use `np.polyfit(log_f, log_psd, 1)` to fit a line; the first coefficient is the slope.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{python}
#| eval: false
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import signal

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

sfreq = 256
duration = 120
n_samples = sfreq * duration

true_exponent = 1.5  # 1/f^1.5 noise (steeper than classical pink)

# Generate 1/f^beta noise
white = rng.standard_normal(n_samples)
freqs_fft = np.fft.rfftfreq(n_samples, d=1 / sfreq)
freqs_fft[0] = 1  # avoid division by zero
# Scale amplitude by f^(-beta/2) so that power ~ f^(-beta)
coloured_filter = freqs_fft ** (-true_exponent / 2)
coloured_noise = np.fft.irfft(
    np.fft.rfft(white) * coloured_filter, n=n_samples
)

# Compute PSD
freqs_psd, psd = signal.welch(coloured_noise, fs=sfreq, nperseg=2048,
                               noverlap=1024)

# Fit in log-log space (exclude DC and very high frequencies)
fit_mask = (freqs_psd >= 1) & (freqs_psd <= 45)
log_f = np.log10(freqs_psd[fit_mask])
log_psd = np.log10(psd[fit_mask])

slope, intercept = np.polyfit(log_f, log_psd, 1)
estimated_exponent = -slope  # slope is negative, exponent is positive

print(f"True aperiodic exponent:      {true_exponent:.2f}")
print(f"Estimated aperiodic exponent: {estimated_exponent:.2f}")
print(f"Error:                        {abs(estimated_exponent - true_exponent):.3f}")

# Plot
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5))

# Left: PSD in log-log space with fit
ax = axes[0]
ax.scatter(log_f, log_psd, s=5, alpha=0.5, color="#2c3e50", label="PSD")
fit_line = slope * log_f + intercept
ax.plot(log_f, fit_line, color="#e74c3c", linewidth=2,
        label=f"Fit: slope = {slope:.2f}")
ax.set_xlabel("log10(Frequency)")
ax.set_ylabel("log10(PSD)")
ax.set_title("Log-log PSD with linear fit")
ax.legend()

# Right: PSD in standard axes
ax = axes[1]
ax.semilogy(freqs_psd, psd, linewidth=1, color="#2c3e50")
ax.set_xlim(0, 50)
ax.set_xlabel("Frequency (Hz)")
ax.set_ylabel("PSD")
ax.set_title(f"PSD of 1/f^{true_exponent} noise")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The estimated exponent should be close to 1.5. In real EEG, the aperiodic exponent typically ranges between 1 and 2, and it changes with age, cognitive state, and neurological conditions. The FOOOF/specparam toolbox automates this fitting and also separates the periodic peaks from the aperiodic background, which gives a cleaner estimate than this simple linear fit.
:::


## Exercise 9: Create topographic maps of alpha and beta band power

Using MNE, create simulated multi-channel data (20 channels with a standard montage) where alpha power (10 Hz) is strongest at occipital channels and beta power (20 Hz) is strongest at central channels. Compute the band power for each channel and use `mne.viz.plot_topomap()` to create scalp maps for each band.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Use `mne.channels.make_standard_montage("standard_1020")` and pick a subset of 20 channels. Create an `mne.Info` object with `mne.create_info(ch_names, sfreq, ch_types="eeg")` and set the montage. To make alpha strong at occipital sites, add a larger-amplitude 10 Hz sine wave to channels like O1, O2, Oz. For beta at central sites, add 20 Hz to C3, C4, Cz. Compute PSD per channel with `scipy.signal.welch`, integrate over each band, and pass the resulting array to `mne.viz.plot_topomap(values, info)`.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{python}
#| eval: false
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import signal
import mne

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

sfreq = 256
duration = 30
n_samples = sfreq * duration
times = np.arange(n_samples) / sfreq

# Define channels and create MNE info
ch_names = [
    "Fp1", "Fp2", "F7", "F3", "Fz", "F4", "F8",
    "T7", "C3", "Cz", "C4", "T8",
    "P7", "P3", "Pz", "P4", "P8",
    "O1", "Oz", "O2",
]
n_channels = len(ch_names)

info = mne.create_info(ch_names=ch_names, sfreq=sfreq, ch_types="eeg")
montage = mne.channels.make_standard_montage("standard_1020")
info.set_montage(montage)

# Simulate data: baseline noise for all channels
data = rng.standard_normal((n_channels, n_samples)) * 0.5

# Add strong alpha (10 Hz) at occipital channels
occipital = ["O1", "Oz", "O2"]
for ch in occipital:
    idx = ch_names.index(ch)
    data[idx] += 2.5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times)

# Add moderate alpha at parietal channels (spatial spread)
parietal = ["P3", "Pz", "P4"]
for ch in parietal:
    idx = ch_names.index(ch)
    data[idx] += 1.0 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times)

# Add strong beta (20 Hz) at central channels
central = ["C3", "Cz", "C4"]
for ch in central:
    idx = ch_names.index(ch)
    data[idx] += 2.0 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 20 * times)

# Compute band power per channel
alpha_power = np.zeros(n_channels)
beta_power = np.zeros(n_channels)

for ch in range(n_channels):
    freqs_psd, psd = signal.welch(data[ch], fs=sfreq, nperseg=1024,
                                  noverlap=512)
    alpha_mask = (freqs_psd >= 8) & (freqs_psd < 13)
    beta_mask = (freqs_psd >= 13) & (freqs_psd < 30)
    alpha_power[ch] = np.trapezoid(psd[alpha_mask], freqs_psd[alpha_mask])
    beta_power[ch] = np.trapezoid(psd[beta_mask], freqs_psd[beta_mask])

# Plot topographic maps
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 5))

im1, _ = mne.viz.plot_topomap(alpha_power, info, axes=axes[0], show=False,
                               cmap="YlOrRd")
axes[0].set_title("Alpha power (8-13 Hz)")
fig.colorbar(im1, ax=axes[0], shrink=0.6)

im2, _ = mne.viz.plot_topomap(beta_power, info, axes=axes[1], show=False,
                               cmap="YlOrRd")
axes[1].set_title("Beta power (13-30 Hz)")
fig.colorbar(im2, ax=axes[1], shrink=0.6)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Print values for verification
print(f"{'Channel':<6} {'Alpha':>10} {'Beta':>10}")
print("-" * 28)
for ch in range(n_channels):
    print(f"{ch_names[ch]:<6} {alpha_power[ch]:>10.3f} {beta_power[ch]:>10.3f}")
```

The alpha topomap should show a hot spot over the occipital region (O1, Oz, O2) with some spread to parietal channels. The beta topomap should show the highest values at central channels (C3, Cz, C4). Topographic maps are one of the most common ways to visualise the spatial distribution of EEG spectral features.
:::


## Exercise 10: Time-frequency decomposition with Morlet wavelets

Create a 10-second signal where the dominant frequency changes over time: 10 Hz in the first half and 20 Hz in the second half, plus some background noise. Use `scipy.signal.morlet2` with `scipy.signal.cwt` to compute the continuous wavelet transform and plot the time-frequency representation. The plot should clearly show the frequency transition at the midpoint.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
`scipy.signal.cwt(signal, scipy.signal.morlet2, widths, w=5)` computes the continuous wavelet transform. The `widths` parameter controls which frequencies are analysed: for a Morlet wavelet with `w` cycles, the relationship is `width = w * sfreq / (2 * np.pi * freq)`. Create an array of target frequencies from 1 to 40 Hz, convert them to widths, and pass them to `cwt`. The output has shape `(n_frequencies, n_samples)`. Plot `np.abs(result)**2` as the power.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{python}
#| eval: false
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import signal as sig

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

sfreq = 256
duration = 10
n_samples = sfreq * duration
times = np.arange(n_samples) / sfreq
midpoint = n_samples // 2

# Signal: 10 Hz in first half, 20 Hz in second half, plus noise
noise = rng.standard_normal(n_samples) * 0.3
oscillation = np.zeros(n_samples)
oscillation[:midpoint] = 1.5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times[:midpoint])
oscillation[midpoint:] = 1.5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 20 * times[midpoint:])
eeg = oscillation + noise

# Define frequencies to analyse and convert to wavelet widths
freqs = np.linspace(2, 40, 100)
w = 6  # number of cycles in the Morlet wavelet
widths = w * sfreq / (2 * np.pi * freqs)

# Compute continuous wavelet transform
cwt_result = sig.cwt(eeg, sig.morlet2, widths, w=w)
power = np.abs(cwt_result) ** 2

# Plot
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10, 7))

# Top: time-domain signal
ax = axes[0]
ax.plot(times, eeg, linewidth=0.4, color="#2c3e50")
ax.axvline(duration / 2, color="#e74c3c", linestyle="--", alpha=0.7,
           label="Frequency switch")
ax.set_xlabel("Time (s)")
ax.set_ylabel("Amplitude")
ax.set_title("Simulated signal: 10 Hz then 20 Hz")
ax.legend()

# Bottom: time-frequency plot
ax = axes[1]
mesh = ax.pcolormesh(times, freqs, power, shading="gouraud", cmap="viridis")
ax.axhline(10, color="white", linestyle="--", linewidth=0.7, alpha=0.7)
ax.axhline(20, color="white", linestyle="--", linewidth=0.7, alpha=0.7)
ax.set_xlabel("Time (s)")
ax.set_ylabel("Frequency (Hz)")
ax.set_title("Time-frequency power (Morlet wavelet)")
fig.colorbar(mesh, ax=ax, label="Power")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(f"Signal: 10 Hz from 0-{duration/2:.0f} s, "
      f"20 Hz from {duration/2:.0f}-{duration:.0f} s")
print(f"Wavelet parameters: w = {w} cycles, "
      f"{len(freqs)} frequencies from {freqs[0]:.0f} to {freqs[-1]:.0f} Hz")
```

The time-frequency plot should show a bright band at 10 Hz in the first half and at 20 Hz in the second half. The transition is not perfectly sharp because the wavelet has a temporal spread (the more cycles you use, the better the frequency resolution but the worse the time resolution). This is the Heisenberg uncertainty principle at work: you cannot have perfect resolution in both time and frequency simultaneously.
:::


## Exercise 11: Simulate event-related desynchronisation (ERD)

Create epoched data that simulates alpha desynchronisation after a visual stimulus. Before time zero (baseline), alpha power is strong. After time zero, alpha power drops. Generate 40 epochs, compute the time course of alpha power (using a sliding window), average across epochs, and quantify the ERD as the percentage drop from baseline. Plot the result.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
For each epoch, create a signal where the alpha amplitude is high before t = 0 and low after t = 0 (e.g., multiply the alpha sine wave by an envelope that steps down at time zero). Add noise to each epoch. To compute the time course of alpha power, bandpass filter the signal into the alpha range (8--13 Hz) and then square the filtered signal (instantaneous power). Smooth with a moving average or use the Hilbert transform (`scipy.signal.hilbert`) to get the analytic amplitude. ERD% = `(active - baseline) / baseline * 100`.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{python}
#| eval: false
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import signal

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

sfreq = 256
epoch_duration = 3.0  # seconds: -1 to +2 s relative to event
n_samples_epoch = int(sfreq * epoch_duration)
times = np.linspace(-1, 2, n_samples_epoch, endpoint=False)
n_epochs = 40

# Create alpha envelope: full amplitude before t=0, reduced after
alpha_freq = 10  # Hz
baseline_amp = 2.0
active_amp = 0.5  # alpha drops after stimulus

epochs = np.zeros((n_epochs, n_samples_epoch))
for i in range(n_epochs):
    # Alpha oscillation with time-varying amplitude
    envelope = np.where(times < 0, baseline_amp, active_amp)
    # Add gradual transition (50 ms ramp)
    ramp_samples = int(0.05 * sfreq)
    zero_idx = np.argmin(np.abs(times))
    ramp = np.linspace(baseline_amp, active_amp, ramp_samples)
    envelope[zero_idx:zero_idx + ramp_samples] = ramp

    alpha = envelope * np.sin(2 * np.pi * alpha_freq * times
                              + rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi))
    noise = rng.standard_normal(n_samples_epoch) * 0.8
    epochs[i] = alpha + noise

# Bandpass filter into alpha band (8-13 Hz)
sos = signal.butter(4, [8, 13], btype="band", fs=sfreq, output="sos")
filtered = np.zeros_like(epochs)
for i in range(n_epochs):
    filtered[i] = signal.sosfiltfilt(sos, epochs[i])

# Compute instantaneous power using the Hilbert transform
analytic = signal.hilbert(filtered, axis=1)
inst_power = np.abs(analytic) ** 2

# Average across epochs
mean_power = inst_power.mean(axis=0)

# Smooth for visualisation (moving average, 100 ms window)
kernel_size = int(0.1 * sfreq)
kernel = np.ones(kernel_size) / kernel_size
smoothed_power = np.convolve(mean_power, kernel, mode="same")

# Compute ERD percentage
baseline_mask = (times >= -0.8) & (times < -0.1)
baseline_power = smoothed_power[baseline_mask].mean()
erd_percent = (smoothed_power - baseline_power) / baseline_power * 100

# Quantify
active_mask = (times >= 0.5) & (times < 1.5)
mean_erd = erd_percent[active_mask].mean()
print(f"Baseline alpha power: {baseline_power:.4f}")
print(f"Mean ERD (0.5-1.5 s): {mean_erd:.1f}%")

# Plot
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10, 7))

ax = axes[0]
ax.plot(times, smoothed_power, linewidth=1.5, color="#2c3e50")
ax.axvline(0, color="#e74c3c", linestyle="--", alpha=0.7, label="Stimulus")
ax.axhline(baseline_power, color="grey", linestyle=":", alpha=0.6,
           label="Baseline level")
ax.set_xlabel("Time (s)")
ax.set_ylabel("Alpha power")
ax.set_title(f"Alpha power time course (n = {n_epochs} epochs)")
ax.legend()

ax = axes[1]
ax.plot(times, erd_percent, linewidth=1.5, color="#8e44ad")
ax.axvline(0, color="#e74c3c", linestyle="--", alpha=0.7, label="Stimulus")
ax.axhline(0, color="grey", linestyle=":", alpha=0.6)
ax.fill_between(times, erd_percent, 0, where=erd_percent < 0,
                alpha=0.3, color="#8e44ad", label="ERD")
ax.set_xlabel("Time (s)")
ax.set_ylabel("ERD (%)")
ax.set_title(f"Event-related desynchronisation (mean ERD = {mean_erd:.1f}%)")
ax.legend()

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

You should see alpha power dropping sharply after time zero and staying low throughout the post-stimulus period. The ERD percentage should be negative (since power decreased), typically around -70% to -80% given our simulation parameters. In real data, the ERD is usually smaller (around -20% to -50%) because the signal-to-noise ratio is lower.
:::


## Exercise 12: Simulate event-related synchronisation (beta rebound)

Create epoched data that simulates a movement-related beta response: beta power drops briefly at time zero (the movement), then rebounds above baseline around 0.5--1.0 seconds later. Generate 40 epochs, compute the time course of beta power (13--30 Hz), and quantify both the ERD (power drop at movement) and the ERS (beta rebound above baseline). Plot the result.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Use a beta envelope that has three phases: (1) baseline level before t = 0, (2) suppression between t = 0 and t = 0.4 s, and (3) rebound above baseline between t = 0.5 and t = 1.0 s, then return to baseline. The ERS percentage is computed the same way as ERD: `(active - baseline) / baseline * 100`, but the result should be positive for the rebound period.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{python}
#| eval: false
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import signal

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

sfreq = 256
epoch_duration = 3.0  # -1 to +2 s
n_samples_epoch = int(sfreq * epoch_duration)
times = np.linspace(-1, 2, n_samples_epoch, endpoint=False)
n_epochs = 40
beta_freq = 20  # Hz

# Build a beta amplitude envelope with ERD then ERS (rebound)
baseline_amp = 1.5
erd_amp = 0.3         # strong suppression during movement
ers_amp = 2.2         # rebound above baseline

envelope = np.ones(n_samples_epoch) * baseline_amp
for i, t in enumerate(times):
    if 0 <= t < 0.4:
        # ERD phase: suppression
        envelope[i] = erd_amp
    elif 0.4 <= t < 0.5:
        # Transition from ERD to ERS
        frac = (t - 0.4) / 0.1
        envelope[i] = erd_amp + frac * (ers_amp - erd_amp)
    elif 0.5 <= t < 1.0:
        # ERS phase: rebound
        envelope[i] = ers_amp
    elif 1.0 <= t < 1.3:
        # Return to baseline
        frac = (t - 1.0) / 0.3
        envelope[i] = ers_amp + frac * (baseline_amp - ers_amp)

# Generate epochs
epochs = np.zeros((n_epochs, n_samples_epoch))
for i in range(n_epochs):
    beta = envelope * np.sin(2 * np.pi * beta_freq * times
                             + rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi))
    noise = rng.standard_normal(n_samples_epoch) * 1.0
    epochs[i] = beta + noise

# Bandpass filter into beta band
sos = signal.butter(4, [13, 30], btype="band", fs=sfreq, output="sos")
filtered = np.zeros_like(epochs)
for i in range(n_epochs):
    filtered[i] = signal.sosfiltfilt(sos, epochs[i])

# Instantaneous power via Hilbert transform
analytic = signal.hilbert(filtered, axis=1)
inst_power = np.abs(analytic) ** 2
mean_power = inst_power.mean(axis=0)

# Smooth
kernel_size = int(0.1 * sfreq)
kernel = np.ones(kernel_size) / kernel_size
smoothed = np.convolve(mean_power, kernel, mode="same")

# Baseline and ERD/ERS
baseline_mask = (times >= -0.8) & (times < -0.1)
baseline_power = smoothed[baseline_mask].mean()
erd_ers_percent = (smoothed - baseline_power) / baseline_power * 100

# Quantify
erd_mask = (times >= 0.1) & (times < 0.35)
ers_mask = (times >= 0.55) & (times < 0.95)
mean_erd = erd_ers_percent[erd_mask].mean()
mean_ers = erd_ers_percent[ers_mask].mean()

print(f"Baseline beta power: {baseline_power:.4f}")
print(f"Mean ERD (0.1-0.35 s): {mean_erd:.1f}%")
print(f"Mean ERS / beta rebound (0.55-0.95 s): {mean_ers:.1f}%")

# Plot
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5))
ax.plot(times, erd_ers_percent, linewidth=1.5, color="#2c3e50")
ax.axvline(0, color="#e74c3c", linestyle="--", alpha=0.7, label="Movement")
ax.axhline(0, color="grey", linestyle=":", alpha=0.6)
ax.fill_between(times, erd_ers_percent, 0, where=erd_ers_percent < 0,
                alpha=0.3, color="#3498db", label="ERD")
ax.fill_between(times, erd_ers_percent, 0, where=erd_ers_percent > 0,
                alpha=0.3, color="#e74c3c", label="ERS (rebound)")
ax.set_xlabel("Time (s)")
ax.set_ylabel("Power change (%)")
ax.set_title("Beta ERD/ERS (movement-related beta dynamics)")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The plot should show beta power dropping below baseline right after the movement (the ERD, shown in blue) and then rebounding above baseline around 0.5--1.0 seconds later (the ERS or "beta rebound", shown in red). This pattern is very well established in motor neuroscience: beta suppression reflects cortical activation during movement, and the rebound is thought to reflect active inhibition or return to a resting state.
:::


## Exercise 13: Compute ERSP with baseline correction

Create epoched data where the spectral content changes over time (strong alpha before the event, strong beta after the event). Compute the spectrogram for each epoch, average across epochs, and apply baseline correction in both dB and percent-change modes. Plot both to see how they differ in scale and interpretability.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
For each epoch, compute the spectrogram with `scipy.signal.spectrogram` (use a short `nperseg` for good time resolution, e.g., 128 samples). Average the spectrograms across all epochs. For baseline correction, take the mean power in each frequency bin during the pre-stimulus interval. In dB mode: `10 * log10(power / baseline)`. In percent-change mode: `(power - baseline) / baseline * 100`. Broadcast the baseline array across the time dimension.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{python}
#| eval: false
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import signal

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

sfreq = 256
epoch_duration = 3.0  # -1 to +2 s
n_samples_epoch = int(sfreq * epoch_duration)
times_epoch = np.linspace(-1, 2, n_samples_epoch, endpoint=False)
n_epochs = 50

# Generate epochs: alpha before event, beta after event
all_Sxx = []

for i in range(n_epochs):
    noise = rng.standard_normal(n_samples_epoch) * 0.5

    # Alpha (10 Hz) in baseline, fading out after event
    alpha_env = np.where(times_epoch < 0, 1.5, 0.3)
    alpha = alpha_env * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times_epoch
                               + rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi))

    # Beta (22 Hz) appears after event
    beta_env = np.where(times_epoch >= 0.2, 1.2, 0.2)
    beta = beta_env * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 22 * times_epoch
                             + rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi))

    epoch = noise + alpha + beta

    # Compute spectrogram for this epoch
    freqs_s, times_s, Sxx = signal.spectrogram(
        epoch, fs=sfreq, nperseg=128, noverlap=112
    )
    all_Sxx.append(Sxx)

# Average spectrogram across epochs
mean_Sxx = np.mean(all_Sxx, axis=0)

# Map spectrogram time bins to actual epoch times
times_s_actual = times_s / sfreq * sfreq + times_epoch[0]
# More direct: spectrogram times start from 0, shift to epoch start
times_s_actual = times_s - 1.0  # shift by 1 s since epoch starts at -1

# Baseline correction
baseline_mask = (times_s_actual >= -0.8) & (times_s_actual < -0.1)
baseline_power = mean_Sxx[:, baseline_mask].mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)

# Avoid division by zero
baseline_power = np.maximum(baseline_power, 1e-10)

# dB correction
ersp_db = 10 * np.log10(mean_Sxx / baseline_power)

# Percent-change correction
ersp_pct = (mean_Sxx - baseline_power) / baseline_power * 100

# Plot
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))

ax = axes[0]
vmax_db = np.percentile(np.abs(ersp_db), 95)
mesh = ax.pcolormesh(times_s_actual, freqs_s, ersp_db,
                     shading="gouraud", cmap="RdBu_r",
                     vmin=-vmax_db, vmax=vmax_db)
ax.axvline(0, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=0.8)
ax.set_ylim(0, 40)
ax.set_xlabel("Time (s)")
ax.set_ylabel("Frequency (Hz)")
ax.set_title("ERSP (dB)")
fig.colorbar(mesh, ax=ax, label="Power (dB re baseline)")

ax = axes[1]
vmax_pct = np.percentile(np.abs(ersp_pct), 95)
mesh = ax.pcolormesh(times_s_actual, freqs_s, ersp_pct,
                     shading="gouraud", cmap="RdBu_r",
                     vmin=-vmax_pct, vmax=vmax_pct)
ax.axvline(0, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=0.8)
ax.set_ylim(0, 40)
ax.set_xlabel("Time (s)")
ax.set_ylabel("Frequency (Hz)")
ax.set_title("ERSP (% change)")
fig.colorbar(mesh, ax=ax, label="Power change (%)")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print("Blue = power decrease relative to baseline")
print("Red = power increase relative to baseline")
print(f"Number of epochs averaged: {n_epochs}")
```

Both plots should show the same pattern: alpha power (around 10 Hz) decreasing after the event and beta power (around 22 Hz) increasing after the event. The dB scale is symmetric on a log scale and compresses large values, which makes it easier to see both small and large changes. The percent-change scale is linear and more intuitive (a value of 200 means power tripled) but can be dominated by large changes in bands with low baseline power.
:::


## Exercise 14: Simulate and extract a P300-like ERP

Create 50 epochs where each trial contains a brief positive peak at 300 ms after the stimulus (the P300 component), simulated as a Gaussian pulse centred at 300 ms at parietal channels, buried in noise. Average across trials to extract the ERP. Plot the ERP waveform and measure the P300 amplitude and latency.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
A Gaussian pulse centred at 300 ms can be created as `amplitude * np.exp(-((times - 0.3)**2) / (2 * width**2))` where `width` controls the duration (try 0.05 for a 50 ms standard deviation). Add random noise to each trial (the noise amplitude should be several times larger than the signal, so that the P300 is invisible in single trials but emerges after averaging). To measure latency, find the time of the maximum in the 200--500 ms window.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{python}
#| eval: false
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

sfreq = 256
epoch_duration = 1.0  # -0.2 to +0.8 s
n_samples = int(sfreq * epoch_duration)
times = np.linspace(-0.2, 0.8, n_samples, endpoint=False)
n_trials = 50

# P300 parameters
p300_latency = 0.300  # seconds
p300_amplitude = 5.0  # microvolts
p300_width = 0.050    # standard deviation of Gaussian (seconds)

# The P300 template (same for every trial)
p300_template = p300_amplitude * np.exp(
    -((times - p300_latency) ** 2) / (2 * p300_width ** 2)
)

# Generate epochs: P300 + noise
noise_amplitude = 15.0  # much larger than the P300
epochs = np.zeros((n_trials, n_samples))
for i in range(n_trials):
    # Add slight jitter to P300 latency (+/- 20 ms)
    jitter = rng.normal(0, 0.02)
    trial_p300 = p300_amplitude * np.exp(
        -((times - (p300_latency + jitter)) ** 2) / (2 * p300_width ** 2)
    )
    noise = rng.standard_normal(n_samples) * noise_amplitude
    epochs[i] = trial_p300 + noise

# Compute the ERP (average across trials)
erp = epochs.mean(axis=0)

# Measure P300 amplitude and latency (search in 200-500 ms window)
window_mask = (times >= 0.2) & (times <= 0.5)
window_times = times[window_mask]
window_erp = erp[window_mask]
peak_idx = np.argmax(window_erp)
measured_latency = window_times[peak_idx]
measured_amplitude = window_erp[peak_idx]

print(f"True P300 latency:     {p300_latency * 1000:.0f} ms")
print(f"Measured P300 latency: {measured_latency * 1000:.1f} ms")
print(f"True P300 amplitude:   {p300_amplitude:.1f} uV")
print(f"Measured P300 amplitude: {measured_amplitude:.2f} uV")
print(f"Number of trials:      {n_trials}")

# Plot
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10, 7))

# Top: single trials (show first 5 and the ERP)
ax = axes[0]
for i in range(5):
    ax.plot(times * 1000, epochs[i], linewidth=0.5, alpha=0.4,
            color="#95a5a6")
ax.plot(times * 1000, erp, linewidth=2, color="#2c3e50", label="ERP (average)")
ax.axvline(0, color="#e74c3c", linestyle="--", alpha=0.7, label="Stimulus")
ax.set_xlabel("Time (ms)")
ax.set_ylabel("Amplitude (uV)")
ax.set_title("Single trials (grey) and ERP (black)")
ax.legend()

# Bottom: ERP with peak marked
ax = axes[1]
ax.plot(times * 1000, erp, linewidth=2, color="#2c3e50")
ax.axvline(0, color="#e74c3c", linestyle="--", alpha=0.7, label="Stimulus")
ax.plot(measured_latency * 1000, measured_amplitude, "o", color="#e74c3c",
        markersize=10, label=f"P300: {measured_amplitude:.1f} uV "
                             f"at {measured_latency * 1000:.0f} ms")
ax.axhline(0, color="grey", linestyle=":", alpha=0.5)
ax.set_xlabel("Time (ms)")
ax.set_ylabel("Amplitude (uV)")
ax.set_title("Extracted ERP with P300 peak")
ax.legend()

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

In the single-trial plot, the P300 is invisible because the noise is three times larger than the signal. After averaging 50 trials, the noise cancels out (it is random and uncorrelated across trials) while the P300 adds up coherently, producing a clear positive peak around 300 ms. The measured latency may differ slightly from 300 ms because of the latency jitter we added to make the simulation more realistic.
:::


## Exercise 15: Compute ERP signal-to-noise ratio

Using the same P300 simulation setup as Exercise 14, compute the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of the ERP as the peak amplitude divided by the standard deviation of the pre-stimulus baseline. Repeat the computation with 10, 25, 50, and 100 trials. Plot SNR as a function of the number of trials and verify that SNR grows approximately as $\sqrt{N}$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
For each number of trials, average that many epochs, measure the peak amplitude in the P300 window (200--500 ms), and measure the standard deviation of the baseline period (-200 to 0 ms). SNR = peak / baseline_std. To check the $\sqrt{N}$ relationship, overlay a scaled $\sqrt{N}$ curve on the plot. The theoretical prediction is that if you double the number of trials, the SNR should increase by a factor of $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.41$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{python}
#| eval: false
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

sfreq = 256
epoch_duration = 1.0
n_samples = int(sfreq * epoch_duration)
times = np.linspace(-0.2, 0.8, n_samples, endpoint=False)

p300_latency = 0.300
p300_amplitude = 5.0
p300_width = 0.050
noise_amplitude = 15.0

# Generate a large pool of epochs
max_trials = 150
all_epochs = np.zeros((max_trials, n_samples))
for i in range(max_trials):
    jitter = rng.normal(0, 0.02)
    trial_p300 = p300_amplitude * np.exp(
        -((times - (p300_latency + jitter)) ** 2) / (2 * p300_width ** 2)
    )
    noise = rng.standard_normal(n_samples) * noise_amplitude
    all_epochs[i] = trial_p300 + noise

# Compute SNR for different numbers of trials
trial_counts = [10, 25, 50, 100]
snr_values = []

baseline_mask = (times >= -0.2) & (times < 0)
p300_mask = (times >= 0.2) & (times <= 0.5)

print(f"{'N trials':>10} {'Peak amp':>10} {'Baseline SD':>12} {'SNR':>8}")
print("-" * 44)

for n in trial_counts:
    erp = all_epochs[:n].mean(axis=0)
    peak_amp = erp[p300_mask].max()
    baseline_std = erp[baseline_mask].std()
    snr = peak_amp / baseline_std
    snr_values.append(snr)
    print(f"{n:>10d} {peak_amp:>10.2f} {baseline_std:>12.3f} {snr:>8.2f}")

snr_values = np.array(snr_values)
trial_counts = np.array(trial_counts)

# Theoretical sqrt(N) curve, scaled to match the first data point
sqrt_curve = snr_values[0] * np.sqrt(trial_counts / trial_counts[0])

# Plot
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
ax.plot(trial_counts, snr_values, "o-", color="#2c3e50", linewidth=2,
        markersize=8, label="Measured SNR")
ax.plot(trial_counts, sqrt_curve, "--", color="#e74c3c", linewidth=1.5,
        label=r"Theoretical $\sqrt{N}$ scaling")
ax.set_xlabel("Number of trials")
ax.set_ylabel("SNR")
ax.set_title("ERP signal-to-noise ratio vs number of trials")
ax.legend()
ax.set_xticks(trial_counts)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Verify sqrt(N) relationship
print(f"\nSNR ratios (each step):")
for i in range(1, len(trial_counts)):
    ratio = snr_values[i] / snr_values[i - 1]
    expected = np.sqrt(trial_counts[i] / trial_counts[i - 1])
    print(f"  {trial_counts[i-1]:>3d} -> {trial_counts[i]:>3d} trials: "
          f"SNR ratio = {ratio:.2f}, expected sqrt ratio = {expected:.2f}")
```

The SNR should roughly follow the $\sqrt{N}$ curve. This is because noise averages out as $1/\sqrt{N}$ (by the central limit theorem), while the signal stays constant. This is why ERP experiments need many trials: to get a 2x improvement in SNR, you need 4x as many trials. The exact values will not be a perfect match because we are working with a finite random sample, but the trend should be clear.
:::


## Exercise 16: Compare eyes-open vs eyes-closed resting-state PSD

Simulate two conditions: eyes-closed (with a strong alpha peak at 10 Hz) and eyes-open (with a weak or absent alpha peak). Compute the PSD for each condition, plot them overlaid, and compute the difference in alpha band power. This is the most basic resting-state EEG paradigm and the alpha blocking effect is one of the oldest findings in EEG research (Berger, 1929).

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Both conditions should have the same 1/f background noise. The eyes-closed condition gets a strong alpha oscillation (amplitude around 2.0) while the eyes-open condition gets a weak one (amplitude around 0.3) or none at all. Compute the PSD for both with the same parameters, plot them on the same axes, and shade the alpha band. Compute the alpha power difference as the integral of the PSD in the 8--13 Hz range for each condition.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{python}
#| eval: false
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import signal

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

sfreq = 256
duration = 60
n_samples = sfreq * duration
times = np.arange(n_samples) / sfreq

def make_eeg(alpha_amp, rng_local):
    """Generate simulated EEG with a given alpha amplitude."""
    white = rng_local.standard_normal(n_samples)
    freqs_fft = np.fft.rfftfreq(n_samples, d=1 / sfreq)
    freqs_fft[0] = 1
    pink_filter = 1 / np.sqrt(freqs_fft)
    pink = np.fft.irfft(np.fft.rfft(white) * pink_filter, n=n_samples)
    pink = pink / pink.std()
    alpha = alpha_amp * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times)
    return pink + alpha

# Generate both conditions
eeg_closed = make_eeg(alpha_amp=2.5, rng_local=rng)
eeg_open = make_eeg(alpha_amp=0.3, rng_local=rng)

# Compute PSDs
freqs_psd, psd_closed = signal.welch(eeg_closed, fs=sfreq, nperseg=1024,
                                      noverlap=512)
_, psd_open = signal.welch(eeg_open, fs=sfreq, nperseg=1024, noverlap=512)

# Compute alpha band power
alpha_mask = (freqs_psd >= 8) & (freqs_psd < 13)
alpha_closed = np.trapezoid(psd_closed[alpha_mask], freqs_psd[alpha_mask])
alpha_open = np.trapezoid(psd_open[alpha_mask], freqs_psd[alpha_mask])
alpha_diff = alpha_closed - alpha_open

print(f"Alpha power (eyes closed): {alpha_closed:.4f}")
print(f"Alpha power (eyes open):   {alpha_open:.4f}")
print(f"Difference:                {alpha_diff:.4f}")
print(f"Ratio (closed / open):     {alpha_closed / alpha_open:.2f}x")

# Plot
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5))
ax.semilogy(freqs_psd, psd_closed, linewidth=1.5, color="#e74c3c",
            label="Eyes closed")
ax.semilogy(freqs_psd, psd_open, linewidth=1.5, color="#3498db",
            label="Eyes open")
ax.axvspan(8, 13, alpha=0.15, color="orange", label="Alpha band (8-13 Hz)")
ax.set_xlim(0, 45)
ax.set_xlabel("Frequency (Hz)")
ax.set_ylabel("PSD")
ax.set_title("Eyes-closed vs eyes-open resting-state PSD")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The eyes-closed PSD should show a prominent alpha peak rising above the 1/f background, while the eyes-open PSD should look much flatter in the alpha range. This "alpha blocking" effect was one of the first EEG phenomena described by Hans Berger in 1929 and is still used today as a basic check that an EEG system is working properly.
:::


## Exercise 17: Compute the theta/beta ratio

Simulate multi-channel EEG data (8 channels). Compute the theta (4--8 Hz) and beta (13--30 Hz) band power for each channel. Calculate the theta/beta ratio (TBR) for each channel and print a summary table. The TBR has been investigated as a potential biomarker in ADHD research, though its clinical utility remains debated.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Generate each channel with a 1/f background and add varying amounts of theta and beta to different channels (to make the results more interesting). Compute the PSD for each channel, integrate over the theta and beta bands, and divide. Format the output as a table with columns for channel name, theta power, beta power, and their ratio.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{python}
#| eval: false
import numpy as np
from scipy import signal

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

sfreq = 256
duration = 60
n_samples = sfreq * duration
times = np.arange(n_samples) / sfreq

ch_names = ["Fp1", "Fp2", "F3", "F4", "C3", "C4", "O1", "O2"]
n_channels = len(ch_names)

# Theta and beta amplitudes per channel (simulate some variability)
# Frontal channels: more theta; Central channels: more beta
theta_amps = {"Fp1": 1.5, "Fp2": 1.4, "F3": 1.2, "F4": 1.3,
              "C3": 0.6, "C4": 0.5, "O1": 0.4, "O2": 0.4}
beta_amps = {"Fp1": 0.4, "Fp2": 0.5, "F3": 0.6, "F4": 0.5,
             "C3": 1.3, "C4": 1.4, "O1": 0.7, "O2": 0.6}

# Generate data
data = np.zeros((n_channels, n_samples))
for ch_idx, ch_name in enumerate(ch_names):
    # Pink noise background
    white = rng.standard_normal(n_samples)
    freqs_fft = np.fft.rfftfreq(n_samples, d=1 / sfreq)
    freqs_fft[0] = 1
    pink_filter = 1 / np.sqrt(freqs_fft)
    pink = np.fft.irfft(np.fft.rfft(white) * pink_filter, n=n_samples)
    pink = pink / pink.std()

    theta = theta_amps[ch_name] * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 6 * times)
    beta = beta_amps[ch_name] * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 20 * times)
    data[ch_idx] = pink + theta + beta

# Compute band powers and TBR
theta_powers = np.zeros(n_channels)
beta_powers = np.zeros(n_channels)

for ch in range(n_channels):
    freqs_psd, psd = signal.welch(data[ch], fs=sfreq, nperseg=1024,
                                  noverlap=512)
    theta_mask = (freqs_psd >= 4) & (freqs_psd < 8)
    beta_mask = (freqs_psd >= 13) & (freqs_psd < 30)
    theta_powers[ch] = np.trapezoid(psd[theta_mask], freqs_psd[theta_mask])
    beta_powers[ch] = np.trapezoid(psd[beta_mask], freqs_psd[beta_mask])

tbr = theta_powers / beta_powers

# Print table
print(f"{'Channel':<8} {'Theta':>10} {'Beta':>10} {'TBR':>8}")
print("-" * 38)
for ch in range(n_channels):
    print(f"{ch_names[ch]:<8} {theta_powers[ch]:>10.4f} "
          f"{beta_powers[ch]:>10.4f} {tbr[ch]:>8.2f}")
print("-" * 38)
print(f"{'Mean':<8} {theta_powers.mean():>10.4f} "
      f"{beta_powers.mean():>10.4f} {tbr.mean():>8.2f}")

# Identify channel with highest TBR
max_ch = ch_names[np.argmax(tbr)]
print(f"\nHighest TBR at channel {max_ch}: {tbr.max():.2f}")
```

Frontal channels (Fp1, Fp2, F3, F4) should have a higher theta/beta ratio because we gave them more theta and less beta. Central channels (C3, C4) should have a lower ratio because of the stronger beta there. In clinical research, elevated frontal TBR has been reported in some ADHD studies, though the finding has not been consistently replicated and the TBR is not currently recommended as a standalone diagnostic measure.
:::


## Exercise 18: Compute frontal alpha asymmetry

Simulate data for two frontal channels (F3 and F4) where alpha power is stronger on the right (F4) than on the left (F3). Compute log-transformed alpha power for each channel and calculate the frontal alpha asymmetry index as `ln(F4) - ln(F3)`. Since greater alpha power reflects less cortical activity (alpha is an "idling" rhythm), a positive asymmetry value indicates relatively greater left cortical activity. Print and interpret the result.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Give F4 a larger alpha amplitude than F3 (e.g., 2.0 vs 1.0). Compute the PSD for both channels, integrate in the alpha band (8--13 Hz), and take the natural log. The asymmetry score is `np.log(alpha_f4) - np.log(alpha_f3)`. A positive value means more alpha on the right, which (counterintuitively) means more cortical activation on the left, because alpha suppression indicates activation.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{python}
#| eval: false
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import signal

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

sfreq = 256
duration = 120
n_samples = sfreq * duration
times = np.arange(n_samples) / sfreq

def make_frontal_eeg(alpha_amp, rng_local):
    """Generate frontal EEG with a given alpha amplitude."""
    white = rng_local.standard_normal(n_samples)
    freqs_fft = np.fft.rfftfreq(n_samples, d=1 / sfreq)
    freqs_fft[0] = 1
    pink_filter = 1 / np.sqrt(freqs_fft)
    pink = np.fft.irfft(np.fft.rfft(white) * pink_filter, n=n_samples)
    pink = pink / pink.std()
    alpha = alpha_amp * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times
                               + rng_local.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi))
    return pink + alpha

# F3 (left): weaker alpha = more active left hemisphere
f3_data = make_frontal_eeg(alpha_amp=1.0, rng_local=rng)

# F4 (right): stronger alpha = less active right hemisphere
f4_data = make_frontal_eeg(alpha_amp=2.0, rng_local=rng)

# Compute PSDs
freqs_psd, psd_f3 = signal.welch(f3_data, fs=sfreq, nperseg=1024,
                                  noverlap=512)
_, psd_f4 = signal.welch(f4_data, fs=sfreq, nperseg=1024, noverlap=512)

# Alpha band power
alpha_mask = (freqs_psd >= 8) & (freqs_psd < 13)
alpha_f3 = np.trapezoid(psd_f3[alpha_mask], freqs_psd[alpha_mask])
alpha_f4 = np.trapezoid(psd_f4[alpha_mask], freqs_psd[alpha_mask])

# Asymmetry index
asymmetry = np.log(alpha_f4) - np.log(alpha_f3)

print(f"Alpha power F3 (left):    {alpha_f3:.4f}")
print(f"Alpha power F4 (right):   {alpha_f4:.4f}")
print(f"ln(alpha F3):             {np.log(alpha_f3):.4f}")
print(f"ln(alpha F4):             {np.log(alpha_f4):.4f}")
print(f"Asymmetry (ln F4 - ln F3): {asymmetry:.4f}")
print()
if asymmetry > 0:
    print("Positive asymmetry: more alpha on the right.")
    print("Interpretation: relatively greater LEFT cortical activity")
    print("(because alpha suppression = cortical activation).")
else:
    print("Negative asymmetry: more alpha on the left.")
    print("Interpretation: relatively greater RIGHT cortical activity.")

# Plot
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
ax.semilogy(freqs_psd, psd_f3, linewidth=1.5, color="#3498db",
            label=f"F3 (left)")
ax.semilogy(freqs_psd, psd_f4, linewidth=1.5, color="#e74c3c",
            label=f"F4 (right)")
ax.axvspan(8, 13, alpha=0.15, color="orange", label="Alpha band")
ax.set_xlim(0, 40)
ax.set_xlabel("Frequency (Hz)")
ax.set_ylabel("PSD")
ax.set_title(f"Frontal alpha asymmetry = {asymmetry:.3f}")
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The asymmetry index should be positive because F4 has more alpha power than F3 by construction. In affective neuroscience, this pattern (relatively greater left frontal activity) has been associated with approach motivation, while the reverse pattern (greater right frontal activity, or negative asymmetry) has been associated with withdrawal motivation. However, the effect sizes in the literature are small and the measure has test-retest reliability issues.
:::


## Exercise 19: Compare Welch and multitaper PSD estimation

Using MNE, create a simulated Raw object with a known spectral structure (alpha peak at 10 Hz over pink noise). Compute the PSD using both Welch's method and the multitaper method via `raw.compute_psd()`. Plot both PSDs on the same axes and discuss their differences.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Create an `mne.io.RawArray` from your simulated data and an `mne.Info` object. Then call `raw.compute_psd(method="welch")` and `raw.compute_psd(method="multitaper")` to get PSD objects. Extract the data with `.get_data()` and the frequencies with `.freqs`. The multitaper estimate uses discrete prolate spheroidal sequences (DPSS, also known as Slepian sequences) as tapers rather than a single windowed segment, which produces smoother estimates with less spectral leakage.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{python}
#| eval: false
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import mne

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

sfreq = 256
duration = 60
n_samples = sfreq * duration
times = np.arange(n_samples) / sfreq

# Generate signal: pink noise + alpha
white = rng.standard_normal(n_samples)
freqs_fft = np.fft.rfftfreq(n_samples, d=1 / sfreq)
freqs_fft[0] = 1
pink_filter = 1 / np.sqrt(freqs_fft)
pink = np.fft.irfft(np.fft.rfft(white) * pink_filter, n=n_samples)
pink = pink / pink.std()

alpha = 2.0 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times)
eeg = pink + alpha

# Create MNE Raw object
info = mne.create_info(ch_names=["Oz"], sfreq=sfreq, ch_types="eeg")
raw = mne.io.RawArray(eeg.reshape(1, -1), info)

# Compute PSD with Welch's method
psd_welch = raw.compute_psd(method="welch", fmin=0.5, fmax=50,
                             n_fft=1024, n_overlap=512)
freqs_w = psd_welch.freqs
psd_w = psd_welch.get_data()[0]  # first (only) channel

# Compute PSD with multitaper method
psd_mt = raw.compute_psd(method="multitaper", fmin=0.5, fmax=50,
                          bandwidth=2.0)
freqs_m = psd_mt.freqs
psd_m = psd_mt.get_data()[0]

# Plot comparison
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10, 8))

# Top: both PSDs overlaid
ax = axes[0]
ax.semilogy(freqs_w, psd_w, linewidth=1.2, color="#3498db",
            label="Welch", alpha=0.8)
ax.semilogy(freqs_m, psd_m, linewidth=1.2, color="#e74c3c",
            label="Multitaper", alpha=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("Frequency (Hz)")
ax.set_ylabel("PSD (V^2/Hz)")
ax.set_title("Welch vs Multitaper PSD estimation")
ax.legend()

# Bottom: ratio of the two
ax = axes[1]
# Interpolate to common frequency grid for comparison
from scipy.interpolate import interp1d
interp_mt = interp1d(freqs_m, psd_m, bounds_error=False, fill_value=np.nan)
psd_m_interp = interp_mt(freqs_w)
ratio = psd_w / psd_m_interp
ax.plot(freqs_w, ratio, linewidth=1, color="#2c3e50")
ax.axhline(1, color="grey", linestyle=":", alpha=0.7)
ax.set_xlabel("Frequency (Hz)")
ax.set_ylabel("Welch / Multitaper ratio")
ax.set_title("Ratio of the two PSD estimates")
ax.set_ylim(0, 3)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print("Both methods should show the same alpha peak at 10 Hz.")
print("The multitaper estimate is typically smoother because it")
print("averages across multiple orthogonal tapers, reducing variance.")
print("Welch's method averages across time segments instead.")
```

Both methods should show the same overall spectral shape: a 1/f slope with an alpha peak at 10 Hz. The multitaper estimate is generally smoother (less wiggly) because it uses multiple orthogonal tapers on each data segment, which reduces variance at the cost of slightly lower frequency resolution. Welch's method achieves variance reduction by averaging across time segments instead. In practice, multitaper is often preferred for short data segments where you cannot afford to split the data into many windows.
:::


## Exercise 20: Three-condition group study with ANOVA

Simulate a three-group experiment with 12 subjects per group: "rest", "task-easy", and "task-hard". Each group has a different mean alpha power level (rest has the most alpha, task-hard the least, reflecting increasing cognitive engagement). Compute alpha band power for each subject, run a one-way ANOVA using `scipy.stats.f_oneway`, and follow up with pairwise t-tests. Create a box plot of alpha power for the three groups.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Give each group a different alpha oscillation amplitude: e.g., 2.0 for rest, 1.2 for task-easy, 0.5 for task-hard. Add between-subject variability by drawing each subject's amplitude from a normal distribution centred at the group mean. Compute the PSD and alpha band power for each subject as in Exercise 4. Use `scipy.stats.f_oneway(group1, group2, group3)` for the ANOVA and `scipy.stats.ttest_ind` for pairwise comparisons. Apply a Bonferroni correction for three comparisons (multiply p-values by 3).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```{python}
#| eval: false
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import signal
from scipy.stats import f_oneway, ttest_ind

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

sfreq = 256
duration = 60
n_samples = sfreq * duration
times = np.arange(n_samples) / sfreq
n_subjects = 12

# Group parameters: (name, mean_alpha_amp, sd_alpha_amp)
groups = [
    ("Rest",      2.0, 0.3),
    ("Task-easy", 1.2, 0.25),
    ("Task-hard", 0.5, 0.2),
]

def simulate_subject_alpha(alpha_amp, rng_local):
    """Simulate one subject and return alpha band power."""
    white = rng_local.standard_normal(n_samples)
    freqs_fft = np.fft.rfftfreq(n_samples, d=1 / sfreq)
    freqs_fft[0] = 1
    pink_filter = 1 / np.sqrt(freqs_fft)
    pink = np.fft.irfft(np.fft.rfft(white) * pink_filter, n=n_samples)
    pink = pink / pink.std()

    eeg = pink + alpha_amp * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times)

    freqs_psd, psd = signal.welch(eeg, fs=sfreq, nperseg=1024, noverlap=512)
    mask = (freqs_psd >= 8) & (freqs_psd < 13)
    return np.trapezoid(psd[mask], freqs_psd[mask])

# Simulate all subjects
group_data = {}
for name, mean_amp, sd_amp in groups:
    powers = []
    for _ in range(n_subjects):
        amp = max(0.1, rng.normal(mean_amp, sd_amp))
        powers.append(simulate_subject_alpha(amp, rng))
    group_data[name] = np.array(powers)

# Print descriptive statistics
print(f"{'Group':<12} {'Mean':>8} {'SD':>8} {'Min':>8} {'Max':>8}")
print("-" * 48)
for name, data in group_data.items():
    print(f"{name:<12} {data.mean():>8.3f} {data.std():>8.3f} "
          f"{data.min():>8.3f} {data.max():>8.3f}")

# One-way ANOVA
f_stat, p_anova = f_oneway(*group_data.values())
print(f"\nOne-way ANOVA: F = {f_stat:.3f}, p = {p_anova:.6f}")

# Pairwise t-tests with Bonferroni correction
print("\nPairwise t-tests (Bonferroni corrected for 3 comparisons):")
group_names = list(group_data.keys())
n_comparisons = 3
for i in range(len(group_names)):
    for j in range(i + 1, len(group_names)):
        g1, g2 = group_names[i], group_names[j]
        t_stat, p_val = ttest_ind(group_data[g1], group_data[g2])
        p_corrected = min(p_val * n_comparisons, 1.0)
        sig = "*" if p_corrected < 0.05 else "n.s."
        print(f"  {g1} vs {g2}: t = {t_stat:.3f}, "
              f"p = {p_val:.6f}, p_corrected = {p_corrected:.6f} {sig}")

# Box plot
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5))
bp = ax.boxplot(
    [group_data[name] for name in group_names],
    labels=group_names,
    patch_artist=True,
    widths=0.5,
)

colours = ["#3498db", "#f39c12", "#e74c3c"]
for patch, colour in zip(bp["boxes"], colours):
    patch.set_facecolor(colour)
    patch.set_alpha(0.5)

# Overlay individual data points
for i, name in enumerate(group_names):
    x = rng.normal(i + 1, 0.04, size=n_subjects)
    ax.scatter(x, group_data[name], color=colours[i], alpha=0.7,
               edgecolors="black", linewidths=0.5, s=30, zorder=3)

ax.set_ylabel("Alpha band power (8-13 Hz)")
ax.set_title(f"Alpha power by condition (ANOVA: F = {f_stat:.1f}, "
             f"p = {p_anova:.2e})")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The ANOVA should be significant (p < 0.05) because the three groups have clearly different alpha power levels by design. The pairwise comparisons should show that the rest group has significantly more alpha than both task conditions, and the task-hard group has significantly less alpha than the task-easy group. In real experiments, the effect of cognitive load on alpha power is well documented: harder tasks produce more alpha suppression, reflecting greater cortical engagement.
:::
